title: Scotch™ Brand launches Scotch Kids® Tape for young creators
summary: New kid-friendly collection supports hands-on creativity, crafting and building for children ages four and up ST. PAUL, Minn., July 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Scotch™ Brand has launched Scotch®...
body_text: New kid-friendly collection supports hands-on creativity, crafting and building for children ages four and up ST. PAUL, Minn. , July 14, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Scotch™ Brand has launched Scotch® Kids Tape to help children create, craft and share their creativity. Designed for kids ages four and up, Scotch® Kids Tape supports crafting, decorating and building projects for young creators. The new line encourages children to confidently apply their imagination and bring their biggest ideas to life with simple materials and without the mess of glue. "Kids are natural creators, builders and problem-solvers," said Amanda Dauphiniais, vice president, Global Product Strategy at 3M. "With the Scotch Kids collection, we're giving children tools designed for hands-on creativity while giving parents a trusted, less-mess solution for everyday projects." Scotch® Kids Tape will help kids: Dream it: Turn their creative ideas into real-world projects Make it: Build and craft with tools designed for little hands Tape it: Finish projects that stick without the mess of glue Share it: Add personal style and display creations with pride From cards and posters to creative builds and colorful decorations, Scotch Kids gives children their own tools for hands-on creativity away from digital screens. For more information about Scotch Kids, visit ScotchBrand.com/kids and view the collection launch video here . About Scotch™ Brand For more than 100 years, Scotch™ Brand has been a leader in adhesive solutions, helping consumers tackle everyday tasks at home, school and work. As the #1 most trusted home and office tape brand*, Scotch™ Brand is designed for crafting and organization to packaging and repairs, with products designed to make life easier while empowering creativity and innovation. * based on Brand Health Survey About 3M 3M (NYSE: MMM) is focused on transforming industries around the world by applying science and creating innovative, customer-focused solutions. Our multi-disciplinary team is working to solve tough customer problems by leveraging diverse technology platforms, differentiated capabilities, global footprint, and operational excellence. Discover how 3M is shaping the future at 3M.com/news.

title: Utz Cheese Balls Brought the Crunch to Beer Bowl 2026 in Support of the Eagles Autism Foundation
summary: Utz sponsored Beer Bowl 2026 in Sea Isle City, N.J., with the Utz x Garage Beer Million Cheese Ball Challenge. The weekend raised $1.26 million for the Eagles Autism Foundation.
body_text: Partnership with Garage Beer Featured the “Million Cheese Ball Challenge” and Fan Activations in Sea Isle City, N.J. HANOVER, Pa. (BUSINESS WIRE) — Utz Quality Foods, LLC (Utz), a subsidiary of Utz Brands, Inc. and the maker of the beloved Utz® Cheese Balls , was an official sponsor of Beer Bowl 2026, the annual charity event hosted by Jason and Kylie Kelce in Sea Isle City, N.J. benefiting the Eagles Autism Foundation . The event featured Utz’s iconic Cheese Balls in the Utz x Garage Beer “Million Cheese Ball Challenge™,” along with fan activations, celebrity appearances and a shared mission of raising funds for autism research and care programs. Held at the Yacht Club of Sea Isle City on June 25, 2026, Beer Bowl 2026 featured competitive team challenges where celebrities and fans competed to help raise funds for the Eagles Autism Foundation. This year, Utz joined Garage Beer, New Heights Productions and Jason and Kylie Kelce to create the Beer Bowl’s cheesiest challenge yet. As part of the event, Utz showcased its signature activation: The Utz x Garage Beer Million Cheese Ball Challenge. Participants jumped into a giant pool filled with over one million Utz Cheese Balls in search of orange Garage Beer-branded ping pong balls. What began as a wildly fun concept became one of the 2026 Beer Bowl’s signature moments. Throughout the event, attendees could also see the Utz-branded boat and visit the Utz fan tent, where Utz snacks were distributed, and fans could design their own custom drink holders and pretzel necklaces. On June 24, Utz participated in the Team 62 event at The Ocean Drive in Sea Isle City, also benefiting the Eagles Autism Foundation. The day featured a dedicated Utz-branded bar with rotating celebrity bartenders, along with Utz snack sampling, iconic Utz Pretzel Necklaces and a live auction featuring select donated items, including a custom cheese ball dispenser from the Utz bar, autographed by Philadelphia Eagles players, team legends and additional attending celebrities. The event surpassed the 2025 record of $1 million, raising $1.26 million for the Eagles Autism Foundation. “Few things go together better than Utz Cheese Balls, Garage Beer and of course, giving back to a worthwhile cause,” said Liza Darnell, Vice President, Marketing Communications at Utz Quality Foods, LLC, a subsidiary of Utz Brands, Inc. “As a snack that doesn’t take itself too seriously, it was only fitting that Utz Cheese Balls were part of this ridiculously fun fundraiser for the Eagles Autism Foundation.” To see content from the event, follow Utz on Facebook , Instagram and TikTok . About Utz Brands, Inc. Utz Brands, Inc. (NYSE: UTZ) manufactures a diverse portfolio of savory snacks through popular brands including Utz®, On The Border® Chips & Dips, Zapp’s®, and Boulder Canyon®, among others. After over a century with a strong family heritage, Utz continues to have a passion for exciting and delighting consumers with delicious snack foods made from top-quality ingredients. Utz’s products are distributed nationally through grocery, mass merchandisers, club, convenience, drug, and other channels. Based in Hanover, Pennsylvania, Utz has multiple manufacturing facilities across the U.S. to serve its growing customer base. For more information, please visit www.utzsnacks.com or call 1-800-FOR-SNAX. About the Eagles Autism Foundation The Eagles Autism Foundation is dedicated to raising funds for innovative research and care programs. By providing the necessary resources to doctors and scientists at leading institutions, the Foundation aims to assist those currently affected by autism as well as future generations. Championed by Eagles Chairman and CEO Jeffrey Lurie, the Eagles Autism Foundation sets out to fund innovative research, drive scientific breakthroughs, and provide critical resources. The Foundation has raised more than $50 million in eight years. About Garage Beer Garage Beer is America’s fastest-growing light beer, now available in all 50 states. Crisp, crushable, and brewed for good times, Garage Beer is a no-nonsense 4% ABV lager with just 95 calories and 3g of carbs. It comes in two crowd-favorite varieties: Classic and Lime. Follow the ride at www.drinkgaragebeer.com , Instagram , and X . Media Contacts SPM Communications Utz Brands, Inc. Utz Brands, Inc. title: Skin Prick Test vs. Blood Test for Allergies: Which Is Better?
summary: Skin prick test vs blood test for allergies: compare accuracy, timing, antihistamine rules, food allergy use, pollen, mold, pet dander, venom, and IgE results.
body_text: If you are trying to figure out what you are allergic to, you will usually run into two main options: a skin prick test at an allergist’s office or a specific IgE blood test through a lab. They can look for many of the same triggers: pollen, dust mites, mold, pet dander, foods, venom, latex, and some medication-related questions. But they are not interchangeable in every situation. Skin prick testing is fast and often preferred by allergists. Blood testing is convenient, quantitative, and useful when skin testing is difficult or not the right fit. Quick summary Skin prick tests and specific IgE blood tests both look for evidence that your immune system is sensitized to an allergen. Skin prick testing usually gives results during the visit and is commonly used by allergists, but antihistamines and some skin conditions can interfere. Blood testing measures allergen-specific IgE from a blood sample, does not require a skin reaction, and can be useful when you cannot stop allergy medications or want a lab-based result. Neither test proves a clinical allergy by itself. The result has to match your symptoms and exposure history. What both tests are trying to answer Both tests are usually asking some version of the same question: Has your immune system made IgE antibodies to this allergen? IgE is the antibody class involved in many immediate allergic reactions. If your body has IgE to cat dander, dust mites, peanut, ragweed, or mold, a test may come back positive. That positive result is called sensitization . Sensitization matters, but it is not the same thing as proven clinical allergy. Some people have positive tests to allergens that do not cause symptoms. Others have symptoms that need a different workup even if the first test is negative. The best allergy diagnosis combines: Your symptoms. Timing, such as minutes after food or seasonal outdoor flares. Exposure pattern, such as pets, bedding, damp rooms, or stings. Test results. Response to avoidance or treatment. Testing is strongest when it confirms a pattern you already see. How a skin prick test works A skin prick test is usually done on the forearm or back. A clinician places small amounts of allergen extract on the skin, then lightly pricks or scratches the surface so the allergen can interact with immune cells in the skin. After about 15 to 20 minutes, the clinician checks for a raised, itchy bump called a wheal. A positive control, often histamine, confirms that your skin can respond. A negative control helps show whether the skin is reacting nonspecifically. Skin prick testing is commonly used for: Pollen allergy. Dust mite allergy. Mold allergy. Cat, dog, and other animal dander. Some food allergy questions. Some venom or medication questions under specialist care. The biggest practical advantage is speed. You can often discuss the pattern with the allergist the same day. How an allergy blood test works An allergy blood test measures allergen-specific IgE in a blood sample. You may see this called specific IgE, sIgE, ImmunoCAP, or historically RAST, though modern labs do not necessarily use the old RAST method. The lab reports whether IgE to a specific allergen is present and often gives a numeric result. That number can help show the degree of sensitization, but it still does not automatically predict symptom severity. Specific IgE blood testing is commonly used for: Food allergens, such as peanut, tree nuts, egg, milk, wheat, soy, sesame, fish, and shellfish. Environmental allergens, such as tree pollen, grass pollen, weed pollen, dust mites, mold, cockroach, and pet dander. Venom allergens, such as bee, wasp, hornet, yellow jacket, or fire ant, depending on lab availability. Situations where skin testing is hard to perform or interpret. The biggest practical advantage is flexibility. You do not need an in-office skin reaction for the test to work, and the sample can be processed like other lab testing. Skin prick test vs blood test: the practical differences Question Skin prick test Specific IgE blood test How results are measured Skin reaction size after allergen exposure. Allergen-specific IgE level in blood. Timing Often read during the appointment. Usually returns after lab processing. Medication issues Antihistamines can suppress the skin response. Often useful when skin testing is not practical, but medication instructions still come from your clinician. Skin conditions Can be harder with severe eczema, widespread rash, dermatographism, or irritated test areas. Does not require a readable skin response. Comfort Multiple small pricks, itching if positive. Standard blood draw. Best use Allergist-led evaluation when same-day interpretation is useful. Lab-based evaluation, targeted panels, medication constraints, or when skin testing is not a good fit. When a skin prick test may be better Skin prick testing is often a strong choice when you are already seeing an allergist and need a hands-on evaluation. It may fit especially well when: You need same-day interpretation. You are evaluating allergic rhinitis, pollen, dust mites, pets, or mold. You can safely stop antihistamines for the recommended window. Your skin is clear enough to test. The allergist wants to test many inhaled allergens during one visit. The result will guide immunotherapy, such as allergy shots or tablets. Skin testing is also useful because the allergist can interpret the result immediately in context. A small positive to one pollen may not matter if your symptoms do not match that season. A strong dust mite result may matter more if your symptoms are worse in bed and in the morning. When a blood test may be better Specific IgE blood testing may be a better fit when skin testing is inconvenient, harder to interpret, or not advised. It may fit especially well when: You cannot stop antihistamines or other medications that could interfere with skin testing. You have eczema, hives, dermatographism, or another skin condition that makes skin results hard to read. You want a lab-based result for specific foods, pollens, molds, pet dander, dust mites, or venom. You need testing for a focused set of allergens rather than a full in-office evaluation. You prefer a blood draw over many skin pricks. You are comparing allergen-specific IgE results over time under clinician guidance. Blood testing is not automatically “better” or “worse.” It answers the IgE sensitization question in a different way. Food allergies: neither test is the final word by itself Food allergy is where interpretation matters most. Skin prick testing and blood IgE testing can both support an IgE-mediated food allergy diagnosis. They are most useful when the history is clear: for example, hives, swelling, wheezing, vomiting, or throat symptoms soon after eating a specific food. But a positive test does not always mean you will react if you eat the food. A negative test does not always explain every symptom. For unclear cases, allergists may use component-resolved testing or a supervised oral food challenge. An oral food challenge is not an at-home experiment. It is done in a medical setting because reactions can be serious. For a deeper food-specific guide, read How to Test for Food Allergies . Environmental allergies: pollen, dust mites, mold, and pets For environmental allergies, both skin prick and blood tests can be useful. The right choice often comes down to logistics, medication use, and the kind of answer you need. Skin prick testing may be efficient if you are seeing an allergist for a full seasonal or indoor allergy evaluation. Blood testing may be easier if you want targeted lab testing for: Tree pollen. Grass pollen. Weed pollen, including ragweed. Dust mites. Cat dander. Dog dander. Cockroach. Indoor molds. Outdoor molds. The key is matching the result to your actual pattern. A dust mite result matters more when symptoms are worse in bed or after cleaning. A ragweed result matters more when symptoms flare in late summer or fall. A mold result matters more when symptoms track with damp or musty spaces. For the environmental-allergy version of this topic, read How to Test for Environmental Allergies . Venom, medication, and severe reactions need specialist guidance Some allergy questions are too high-stakes for self-directed testing. If you have had throat swelling, trouble breathing, fainting, low blood pressure, or a severe whole-body reaction after a sting, food, medication, or latex exposure, talk with a clinician or allergist. Testing may still involve skin testing, blood testing, or challenge procedures, but the safety plan matters as much as the lab result. Medication allergy is especially specific. For example, some drug allergy workups use skin testing or challenge procedures under specialist supervision, while ordinary blood allergy testing may not answer the question. Which test should you choose? Use this as a practical starting point: Your situation Often better starting point Why Seasonal congestion, itchy eyes, or sneezing Either skin prick or specific IgE blood testing Both can assess pollen and respiratory allergens. Symptoms at home, in bed, around pets, or in damp rooms Either skin prick or specific IgE blood testing Both can assess dust mites, pet dander, mold, and cockroach. You cannot stop antihistamines Specific IgE blood testing Antihistamines can suppress skin test reactions. Severe eczema, widespread rash, or dermatographism Specific IgE blood testing Skin testing may be hard to perform or interpret. Clear immediate food reaction Allergist-guided testing, often skin prick and/or blood IgE Food allergy decisions need history-based interpretation. Possible venom or medication allergy Allergist-guided testing Testing strategy and safety planning are more specialized. What neither test can tell you Neither skin prick testing nor blood IgE testing can answer every allergy-adjacent question. They do not prove: That a positive allergen is definitely causing your symptoms. That a food is unsafe to eat without clinical context. That a negative result rules out every possible reaction. That a home has mold, dust mites, or pet dander present. That chronic digestive symptoms are caused by allergy. That IgG or IgG4 food sensitivity results diagnose allergy. This is why the symptom story matters. A test result is a clue. It is strongest when it lines up with real exposure and real symptoms. How Mito fits in Mito offers lab-based allergy testing organized by trigger category, including food, seasonal, indoor, mold, pet, venom, and exposure-related testing. That makes specific IgE blood testing easier to browse when you already have a likely category in mind. If your symptoms suggest a severe food reaction, venom reaction, medication reaction, or uncontrolled asthma, start with a clinician or allergist. For lower-risk questions, such as “could dust mites, mold, pet dander, pollen, or a specific food be part of this pattern?”, specific IgE blood testing can be a practical way to start. Browse Mito allergy tests . The bottom line Skin prick tests and allergy blood tests can both identify IgE sensitization. Skin prick testing is fast and often preferred in an allergist’s office. Blood testing is flexible, lab-based, and useful when skin testing is inconvenient, medication-limited, or hard to interpret. The better test is the one that fits your symptoms, risk level, and practical constraints. The most important step is not testing the largest number of allergens. It is choosing the test that matches the pattern you are actually trying to explain.
